segments.title: Primary sources reveal an argument's foundation
segments.body: The source list gives an early indication of what supports a book's analysis. Primary sources include contemporary accounts by people at the events and government records compiled from those close to them. They remain one step removed from the event itself, yet they connect the author to firsthand information. A strong primary-source base therefore helps a reader see how directly the argument rests on contemporary evidence. It also leaves the author's own analysis visible instead of filtering it through earlier historians' interpretations.

evidence.note: The transcript explains how contemporary accounts and official records indicate a primary-source basis.

segments.summary: A source list rich in contemporary testimony and official records shows how closely a historian's argument rests on the events and people involved.

segments.title: Secondary accounts add another layer of analysis
segments.body: Secondary accounts include contemporary diarists who were not present at the events and later books written from primary material. A book built mainly on them filters its argument through earlier writers' choices and analysis. It may therefore be examining what others have said about an event more than reconstructing the event directly. That remains worthwhile, but it is a different kind of historical work. Reading the source list first tells the reader which kind of contribution to expect.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts secondary accounts with direct analysis of what happened.

segments.summary: A bibliography dominated by secondary accounts can still support worthwhile history, but it shows that the author's interpretation passes through earlier analyses.

segments.title: Ask who supplied the information
segments.body: Source criticism becomes an everyday way to evaluate information, rather than a habit reserved for choosing history books. When reading news or watching television, the first question is where the information came from. A report about a scientific breakthrough might draw on the scientists, their public-relations team, a sponsoring company, or a government sponsor. Each route can shape how much of the underlying information reaches the audience. The immediate issue is less whether someone is telling the truth than whether the account is full enough to support its framing.

evidence.note: The transcript extends source questioning to news and scientific public-relations chains.

segments.summary: The habit of asking who supplied a claim helps readers assess how full an account is, whether they are reading history, news, or a scientific announcement.
